**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 3 (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic maps, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

### (a)(ii) Null hypothesis (2 marks)

$H_0$: **there is no significant relationship (correlation) between the slope angle and the soil depth on the farm at Wotutu; any apparent relationship is due to chance.** (The alternative hypothesis $H_1$: there is a significant relationship, steeper slopes having thinner soils.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) (i) Calculate the correlation between slope angle and soil depth using the Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient ($r_s$) formula stated as:

$$r_s = 1 - \frac{6\sum d^2}{n^3 - n}$$

where $r_s$ is the Spearman correlation coefficient, $d^2$ is the square difference in rank, and $n$ is the number of sites. **(4 marks)**

Study the levels of significance below.

| N | Significance level, 95% confidence level | Significance level, 99% confidence level |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 1.00 | - |
| 5 | 0.90 | 1.00 |
| 6 | 0.83 | 0.94 |
| 7 | 0.71 | 0.89 |
| 8 | 0.64 | 0.83 |
| 9 | 0.60 | 0.78 |
| 10 | 0.56 | 0.75 |
| 12 | 0.51 | 0.71 |
| 14 | 0.46 | 0.65 |
| 16 | 0.43 | 0.60 |

(ii) State the statistical significance of the result in (b) (i). **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
### (b)(i) Calculation of $r_s$ (4 marks)

Formula: $r_s = 1 - \dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n^3 - n}$, with $n = 10$ sites and $\sum d^2 = 279$.

$$r_s = 1 - \frac{6 \times 279}{10^3 - 10}$$

$$r_s = 1 - \frac{1674}{990} = 1 - 1.691 = -0.69$$

**Result: $r_s = -0.69$** (to 2 decimal places; more exactly $-0.691$).

(Formula and substitution 2 marks, correct arithmetic 1 mark, result with its negative sign 1 mark.) The negative sign shows an **inverse (negative) correlation**: when slope angle increases, soil depth decreases. Note that two pairs of tied ranks are present (the formula is then only an approximation, which is acceptable at this level).

### (b)(ii) Statistical significance (3 marks)

- Number of sites $n = 10$; the table gives the **critical values 0.56 at the 95 % level and 0.75 at the 99 % level**.
- The absolute value $|r_s| = 0.69$ is **greater than 0.56** and **less than 0.75**.
- Conclusion: the correlation is **statistically significant at the 95 % confidence level** (there is at most a 5 % probability that it happened by chance), but it is **not significant at the 99 % level**. The null hypothesis is therefore **rejected at 95 %** and the alternative accepted: there is a significant strong negative relationship between slope angle and soil depth.

questions.corrige_markdown:
### (c)(i) Description and explanation (5 marks)

**Description.** The data show a **fairly strong negative relationship** ($r_s = -0.69$): as the slope angle increases, the soil gets thinner.

- The **gentlest slopes** have the deepest soils: sites 10 ($3^\circ$) and 5 ($5^\circ$) both have 60 cm and site 1 ($6^\circ$) has 58 cm.
- The **steepest slopes** have shallow soils: sites 8 ($27^\circ$) and 6 ($23^\circ$) have 25 cm.
- **Anomalies:** site 4 ($14^\circ$) has the thinnest soil (18 cm) and site 3 ($13^\circ$) has only 20 cm although their slopes are moderate, while sites 7 and 9 ($19^\circ$ and $20^\circ$) have 30 cm and 29 cm, deeper than sites 3 and 4 on gentler slopes. Such results explain why the coefficient is not close to $-1$.

**Explanation.**

1. On **steep slopes**, gravity, **surface runoff (sheet wash)**, rainsplash and soil creep remove weathered material faster than it forms, so little soil accumulates; infiltration is low and the water runs off.
2. On **gentle slopes** and at the foot of slopes, runoff is slow, **infiltration** is high, material washed from higher ground is **deposited** and weathering and organic matter build up, so a deep soil forms.
3. **Other factors** explain the anomalies: type and resistance of the parent rock, vegetation cover and root binding, cultivation and ploughing along or across the slope, local hollows or rock outcrops, and drainage conditions.

The study relates to a farm in a humid area near Buea, where heavy rainfall increases erosion on bare slopes.

### (c)(ii) Importance of Spearman's coefficient (2 marks) - any two

- It measures the **strength and direction** (positive or negative) of the relationship between two sets of data in a single figure between $-1$ and $+1$.
- It allows the **statistical significance** of the relationship to be tested, so that the researcher can accept or reject the null hypothesis, instead of relying on a visual impression.
- It can be used with **small samples** and with data that are **not normally distributed**, because it uses ranks, and the **effect of extreme values is reduced**.
- It is **simple and quick** to calculate, even by hand.
